title: Doubly efficient \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
formal: For every uniform deterministic polynomial-space decider \(M\) and every time-constructible bound \(T(n)\ge n+2\) on its running time, does the language \(L(M)\) have a uniform classical single-prover interactive proof with a verifier running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time and an honest prover running in \(\operatorname{poly}(T(n))\) total time, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) against every cheating prover? The quantifier covers the full time range, rather than only \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\).
why: The class equality IP = PSPACE says that polynomial space can be verified efficiently, but does not by itself control the cost of generating the proof relative to the original computation. The target asks whether that prover overhead can always be polynomial while retaining soundness against an unlimited adversary.

progress.text: Berger, Goyal, Hong and Kalai extend doubly efficient protocols to \(T(n)=n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}\), as recorded in the June 2026 paper’s comparison.

ECCC revision 1 gives the \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time range; Section 4, Theorem 5 and Corollary 1 specify the prover and verifier bounds. The revision notice says the change from the original report fixes title encoding.
A separate report constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions. Its abstract explicitly limits soundness to cheating provers of bounded circuit size.

context_blocks.text: The card retains its earlier time-constructible, uniform single-prover formulation and constant error gap. The June 2026 source constructs public-coin protocols with perfect completeness, which meet a stronger interface within the time range it covers. The source’s particular round format is not imposed on a solution of this card.

Polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed computation and time bound, but the programs and exponents must remain fixed over all input lengths. Time constructibility does not give the verifier a free time-bound oracle; any work it performs is included in its own bound.

The checked June paper covers polynomial-space computations with \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\). Its more general theorem has verifier time \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log_2 T})}S^2\operatorname{poly}(\sigma,\log S)\), where \(S\) is the space bound and \(2^{-\sigma}\) is the soundness error. This factor is not polynomial in \(n\) throughout the full time range.

The two running-time requirements concern the honest participants. Restricting honest proof generation does not restrict cheating strategies. This distinguishes the question from argument systems whose soundness relies on an adversary’s computational limitations.

The July 2026 one-way-function result gives efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computation, with a stated bound on the size of cheating provers. It does not give the information-theoretic soundness required here.

answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal protocol-existence assertion with all stated uniformity, total worst-case running-time, completeness and soundness requirements, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. A result covering only a restricted time range, an efficient verifier with no honest-prover bound, or computational soundness under a cryptographic assumption does not settle the assertion. The time bounds are asymptotic resource requirements, not numerical quantities with \(1/100\) additive tolerance.
definitions:
Fix the standard bit-cost model of deterministic multitape Turing machines with a read-only binary input tape. A decider halts and accepts or rejects on every binary input. For each fixed \(M\), there is a polynomial \(q\) such that on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), \(M\) uses at most \(q(n+2)\) work-tape cells and takes at most \(T(n)\) steps. The same machine must satisfy both bounds. Here \(T:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) is time-constructible in the following convention: some fixed deterministic machine, on unary input \(1^n\), outputs the binary representation of \(T(n)\) within \(K T(n)\) steps for a constant \(K\). The requirement \(T(n)\ge n+2\) merely absorbs bounded lengths. Define \(L(M)=\{x:M\text{ accepts }x\}\).

An interactive proof consists of two fixed finite programs, an honest prover \(P\) and a verifier \(V\), which both receive only the common input \(x\) and exchange finite binary messages. They may use independent private fair random bits. A protocol may expose verifier randomness through its messages, but public coins and perfect completeness are not extra requirements. The machines know their fixed protocol and may incorporate the fixed descriptions of \(M\) and a constructor for \(T\). They receive no advice depending on input length, trusted preprocessing, shared secret, additional witness, oracle, or separately supplied value of \(T(n)\).

For each fixed \(M,T\), there must be constants \(C,a,b\ge1\) and one such pair \(P,V\), all independent of \(n,x\), satisfying these bounds for every input. The verifier's total number of bit operations is at most \(C(n+2)^a\), on every random tape and against every possible sequence of prover messages. It accepts or rejects within that bound. The total number of messages, all transmitted or read message bits and verifier random bits are charged to this bound; malformed or oversized messages may be rejected. The honest prover's total number of bit operations during an interaction with \(V\) is at most \(C(T(n)+2)^b\), on every choice of both random tapes, including inputs outside the language. All input-dependent preprocessing, message generation and communication are included. No separate restriction to polynomial prover space is imposed.

Completeness requires
\[
\Pr[\langle P,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3
\quad\text{for every }x\in L(M),
\]
where the probability is over both machines' independent random bits. Soundness requires, for every \(x\notin L(M)\) and every cheating strategy \(P^*\),
\[
\Pr[\langle P^*,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\le1/3.
\]
A cheating strategy can depend arbitrarily on \(x\) and its visible transcript and can perform unlimited computation; it has no access to unexposed verifier randomness. It may be randomized, with its private randomness independent of the verifier's. There is only one prover, and no computational assumption restricts soundness.

The quantifier order is: for every fixed pair \(M,T\) satisfying the time and polynomial-space premises, there exist \(P,V,C,a,b\) that work for all inputs and lengths. No algorithm transforming descriptions of \(M,T\) into protocols is additionally demanded. The prover bound refers to the specified \(T(n)\), not to an unrestricted exponential in the space bound. The verifier bound remains polynomial in the original input length even when \(T\) is superquasipolynomial.

importance.reason: Tests the efficiency limits of the IP = PSPACE phenomenon when both verifier and prover costs matter, across the full time range.

category_assignment.reason: The problem refines IP=PSPACE through honest-prover and verifier running times, rather than propositional proof length.

sentences: An interactive proof lets a verifier check a computation through a conversation with one prover.
The question asks for a verifier polynomial in input length and an honest prover polynomial in the specified computation time for every polynomial-space decider.
The protocol must be uniform across input lengths and must remain sound against arbitrarily powerful cheating strategies.
The checked June 2026 theorem covers quasipolynomial computation times, while the card asks for the full time range.
A resolution would strengthen IP = PSPACE by controlling proof-generation overhead without replacing information-theoretic soundness with a cryptographic assumption.
